# A message queue as an extension

[pgmq](https://github.com/pgmq/pgmq) is a queue in the style of Amazon SQS, written as a Postgres
extension in plain SQL. A queue is a table, and every operation is a function: `pgmq.send`,
`pgmq.read`, `pgmq.delete`, `pgmq.archive`. There is no client library and no worker framework, so
anything that can run SQL can produce or consume, from psql to a trigger to a Go service.

## The visibility timeout

The idea that carries everything is the **visibility timeout**. `read` does not mark a message as
owned by anyone. It pushes the message's `vt` timestamp into the future, and until then nobody else
sees it:

```sql
SELECT pgmq.create('jobs');
SELECT pgmq.send('jobs', '{"page": "orm/quickstart"}');
SELECT msg_id, read_ct, message FROM pgmq.read('jobs', 30, 1);   -- hidden for 30 s
SELECT pgmq.archive('jobs', 1);                                  -- done: moved to pgmq.a_jobs
```

A consumer that finishes deletes or archives the message. A consumer that crashes does nothing,
and when `vt` passes the message is there again, with `read_ct` counting the attempt. In the
notebook, consumer A reads with a 2 second timeout and dies; consumer B gets nothing at first, and
the same message 2.2 seconds later with `read_ct` 2.

Delivery is therefore **at least once**. A consumer that is merely slow is treated like one that
crashed, so long work calls `set_vt` to extend its lease: in the notebook a 3 second job on a 2
second timeout loses its message to a second consumer, and keeps it when it extends every half
second. `pop`, which reads and deletes in one statement, is the at-most-once alternative.

## Building the rest from two columns

pgmq has no retry policy. It has `read_ct` and `set_vt`, which are enough to write one:

```python
for msg_id, read_ct, message in read_batch():
    try:
        handle(message)
        archive(msg_id)
    except Exception:
        if read_ct >= 3:
            with conn.transaction():       # in exactly one of the two queues, always
                send("jobs_dead", message)
                delete("jobs", msg_id)
        else:
            set_vt(msg_id, 2 ** read_ct)  # backoff
```

The notebook runs this against a flaky and a broken page: the flaky one succeeds on its second
attempt, the broken one lands in the dead-letter queue after its third.

## What else it does

- **Many consumers**: `read` claims with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside one `UPDATE`. Four threads
  on 400 messages took exactly 100 each, none twice, in 0.12 s.
- **Waking up**: `read_with_poll` loops inside Postgres; `enable_notify_insert` adds a trigger that
  sends `NOTIFY` on `pgmq.q_<name>.INSERT`. Measured from send to receipt, NOTIFY took about 12 ms
  (median of 8), while polling took up to its interval.
- **Delayed messages**: `send(queue, msg, delay)` sets `vt` ahead at insert.
- **FIFO groups**: an `x-pgmq-group` header and `read_grouped`; a group's messages come out in order
  and one at a time. One plain `read` on the same queue ignores groups, so every consumer has to use
  the grouped functions.
- **Topics**: `bind_topic('orders.*.paid', 'payments')` and `send_topic('orders.eu.paid', msg)`,
  with RabbitMQ-style wildcards (`*` one word, `#` any number after a dot).
- **Archive tables**: `pgmq.a_<name>` keeps every archived message with `archived_at`, a free audit
  log.

## pgmq and pgqueuer side by side

Both claim work with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and neither holds a lock while the work runs. They
differ in how a claim expires and in where the logic lives.

| | pgmq | pgqueuer |
|---|---|---|
| what it is | a Postgres extension, SQL functions | a Python library over plain tables |
| a claim | `read` pushes `vt` ahead | dequeue sets `status = 'picked'` |
| a claim expires | when `vt` passes, unless the consumer calls `set_vt` | when the worker's heartbeat is older than `heartbeat_timeout`, refreshed for you |
| consumers | any language with a Postgres driver | Python asyncio workers |
| waking up | `read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` and `LISTEN` | `LISTEN ch_pgqueuer`, always on |
| retries | by hand, from `read_ct` and `set_vt` | built in, with `on_failure="hold"` |
| extras | archive, topics, FIFO groups, partitioned queues | dedupe keys, fleet-wide limits, cron schedules |

pgmq suits a queue shared by several languages or services, or fed from SQL itself, where an
SQS-shaped API is the point. pgqueuer suits a Python application that wants a worker framework with
retries, limits and schedules already written.

::: {.callout-note}
